Nestlings of the Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) emerge from their eggs after an incubation period of approximately 40 days [ab = approximately 40 days] at 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. This extended development occurs within eggs that, at the point of laying, have a volume of roughly 66.5 milliliters , based on measurements taken from eggs in Norwegian colonies. The initial wet weight of these eggs averages 65.8 grams [Ww0 = 65.8 grams], though values can range from 61.9 to 70.4 grams [Ww0 = 61.9 to 70.4 grams] depending on the specific colony. The hatchlings themselves, which are semi-precocial and covered in down, exit the shell at a typical wet weight of 44 grams [Wwb = 44 grams]. This birth mass shows considerable inter-colony variation, spanning from 39.7 to 50 grams [Wwb = 39.7 to 50 grams]. The relatively large investment per offspring, reflected in both the egg volume and the considerable hatchling mass, is a characteristic feature of this species, which produces only a single egg per breeding attempt.

Atlantic puffins exhibit a slow and deliberate pace of life, a strategy that is underscored by their energetic physiology and lifespan. At rest, an adult puffin of ultimate size consumes oxygen at a basal metabolic rate of approximately 610.4 milliliters per hour [JOi = approximately 610.4 milliliters per hour], when measured at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This measurement from respirometry trials provides a baseline for the resting metabolic demands required to sustain vital functions. The species also demonstrates remarkable longevity; the oldest documented individuals in the wild have reached an age of approximately 40.8 years [am = approximately 40.8 years] at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a considerable lifespan relative to many other alcids. Such long-term survival is likely linked to their low annual reproductive output and the intense competition for breeding territories on coastal cliffs.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active breeding season (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), the single egg laid per breeding attempt represents the species' maximum reproductive output. Females lay one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch] and commit to one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually], resulting in a lifetime strategy of low fecundity. This annual constraint is a defining feature of the species' life history, as each single clutch that a female lays [F_R_i = annual constraint is a defining feature of the species' life history, as each single clutch that a female lays] must be successfully incubated and the chick fed until fledging. This low fecundity is balanced by the relatively high investment in each chick's early development. Following their time in the burrow, the young must achieve a key developmental milestone before they can leave the colony. The time from hatching to fledging, when the chick is capable of sustained flight, averages about 45 days after hatching [tx = about 45 days after hatching] at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], although this duration can vary between 34 and 83 days depending on conditions.

The rigorous schedule of the breeding season demands a high level of physical condition in the adult birds. Breeding adults, during the demanding summer months, attain a mean ultimate wet weight of approximately 436 grams [Wwi = approximately 436 grams], though the population displays wide variation, with individuals ranging from 350 to 555 grams depending on sex, health, and colony-specific foraging conditions. Wing length, a standard metric of structural size in seabird research, averages 16.7 centimeters [Li = 16.7 centimeters] in adults, a measurement that itself fluctuates geographically, with colony means spanning from 16.2 to 17.3 centimeters [Li = 16.2 to 17.3 centimeters]. This morphological variation, combined with body mass differences, illustrates the adaptability of the species to local marine environments and the varying quality of prey resources across its North Atlantic range.

After successfully fledging, young puffins do not breed immediately. Rather, they undergo a prolonged juvenile and sub-adult phase that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity, occurring approximately 135 days after birth [tp = approximately 135 days after birth], at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Inter-annual and inter-colony variation, however, can push the timing of gonadal maturation into a range spanning from 34 to 83 days [tp = 34 to 83 days]. Once fully mature, a young puffin will still not breed immediately; the onset of first reproduction, which involves securing a burrow and a mate, typically occurs at about 1460 days after hatching [tR = about 1460 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This delay highlights the intense competition for limited nesting space and the years required to achieve sufficient foraging experience to support a chick.
